newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS-Gold market unfazed by Buba tussle with Bonn.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Gold market unfazed by Buba tussle with Bonn.

text.p: Gold futures in New York were unfazed by the emerging tussle between the German Bundesbank and Bonn politicians over revaluing the country's official yellow metal reserves, dealers said.
"This is having no real impact at the moment," Greg Drury of Mitsui USA said. "We have to wait to see if it blows up into a bigger confrontation and then there may be some impact."

In early afternoon trading on New York's COMEX, June gold barely changed following the Bundesbank statement issued 1300 EDT / 1700 GMT. June was down 40 cents at $344.30 an ounce, traded $345.60 to $343.10.
Germany's central bank said Wednesday it rejected Bonn's plans to revalue gold assets to help boost its finances in the run up to European Economic and Monetary Union.
Andy Smith, bullion analyst a Union Bank of Switzerland, said there could be many positives for gold from the tussle.

"Either there's a postponement until this issue is sorted out, which is good for gold as a relief factor from sales. Or if it does go ahead on some balance sheet massaging basis, the need for gold sales from anybody is reduced, if Germany can do it," Smith said.
"And in the meantime the attack on the Bundesbank has raised investor fears generally about inflation outlooks, which is positive," Smith added.
The gold market on Wednesday was largely focused on surging palladium and platinum prices, dealers said.
Bullion barely budged on the news from Germany.
"Gold is just being pushed around a bit by platinum and palladium. There is no immediate reaction here (to the German bank's statement)," a COMEX gold floor source said.
Jeffery Christian of CPM Group said that gold may benefit in the medium term because of the harm being done to credibility of the German Finance Ministry and Bundesbank.
"The major implication of all this is that the Ministry of Finance has really weakened the credibility of the Bundesbank in the eyes of the financial markets," Christian said.
"In so far as those things are not so good for the Deutsche mark, and they are not good for the prospects of monetary union, it's good for gold," Christian said.
Mitsui's Drury said of the Germany revaluation spat:"Until there is selling of gold involved, or some statement to that effect, this story is largley discounted in the market now, I would think."
